collection_summary: Adapted / narrowed from seed #19 in datasets/pkdb_bench/docs/example_questions.txt ('For each major scientific discipline, list the 5 most influential scientists with their nationality, approximate era, and most important contribution.'). Cycle-0 staging applied the cycles 1-3 lessons from twentieth_century_decade_inventions and cycles 1-2 from world_religions_top5_holy_sites: (a) selection framing ('notable foundational' not 'most influential' — initial cycle-0 used 'widely-cited' but the cycle-2 audit flagged that as still implying citation/ranking evidence which the staged sources do not provide; cycle-2 retitled to 'notable foundational'); (b) PK = (Discipline, Scientist) with List Position non-key; (c) per-scientist Wikipedia article cited for each row's biographical values from cycle 0. Cycle-1 audit added two further fixes: (d) added 5 per-discipline 'List of [Xists]' Wikipedia articles as discipline-membership universe anchors so the row universe is source-defined-membership + curator-display selection rather than purely curator selection (cycle-0 had only the universe-anchor 'Branches of science' + per-scientist articles, which the auditor flagged as insufficient to define the 5-per-discipline row universe); (e) replaced James Watson (1928-2025) with Francis Crick (1916-2004) for the Biology row 5 to keep the Era column cutoff-stable for pre-2025 LLMs while preserving the DNA-double-helix attribution (Crick is the universally co-credited co-author of the 1953 Nature paper). Tier B (manual_wikipedia) extraction. Universe is 5 disciplines (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Astronomy) anchored to Wikipedia 'Branches of science'. Cycle-1 source_count = 31 (1 disciplines anchor + 25 per-scientist articles + 5 per-discipline membership-universe list articles). Result: 5 disciplines x 5 scientists = 25 rows x 6 columns, composite PK on (Discipline, Scientist), 0 duplicate PKs. Multi-attribute (Nationality, Era, Contribution) over the per-discipline partition exercises the calibration goal of scaled_enumeration: universally-known foundational figures (Newton, Einstein, Darwin, Galileo, Copernicus, Curie, Pasteur, Mendel, Maxwell) are very strong recall signals, while less-universally-known figures (Faraday, Dalton, Linnaeus, Riemann, Hilbert, Herschel) progressively exercise the confidence gradient.
source_coverage_notes:
Thirty-one Wikipedia source URLs combine to support the universe + per-discipline membership + per-scientist attribution values (cycle-1 audit fix; was 26 at cycle-0 staging). One discipline-universe anchor ('Branches of science') + 5 per-discipline membership universe anchors ('List of [Xists]' articles, added at cycle-1) + 25 per-scientist value articles (5 per discipline × 5 disciplines). The cycle-1 audit found that the cycle-0 source plan supported discipline names and per-scientist biographical values but did not define the 5-scientist-per-discipline row universe; cycle-1 added the 5 'List of [Xists]' articles to anchor the discipline-membership universe (which scientists count as physicists / chemists / biologists / mathematicians / astronomers per Wikipedia). The 5-per-discipline selection from each membership universe is curator's display choice of notable foundational figures, documented in decision_log.

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branches_of_science): universe. Classifies all 5 disciplines (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Astronomy) as major scientific disciplines per the 'commonly divided into three major groups' (Formal / Natural / Social) hierarchy. Verbatim: Physics + Chemistry + Astronomy listed under Natural-Sciences/Physical-Science; Biology under Natural-Sciences/Life-Science; Mathematics under Formal-Sciences.
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton): value (Physics row 1). Verbatim: Newton was 'an English polymath' (1643-1727); 'achieved the first great unification in physics' through his laws of motion and universal gravitation.
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday): value (Physics row 2). Verbatim: Faraday was 'an English scientist' (1791-1867); 'he discovered electromagnetic induction, diamagnetism, and the laws of electrolysis'.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell): value (Physics row 3). Verbatim: Maxwell was a 'Scottish physicist' (1831-1879); 'responsible for the classical theory of electromagnetic radiation, which was the first theory to describe electricity, magnetism and light as different manifestations of the same phenomenon'.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein): value (Physics row 4). Verbatim: 'Albert Einstein (14 March 1879 – 18 April 1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the theory of relativity'.
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niels_Bohr): value (Physics row 5). Verbatim: Bohr 'was a Danish theoretical physicist' (1885-1962); 'made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922'.
- source_urls[6] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier): value (Chemistry row 1). Verbatim: 'French chemist' (1743-1794); 'noted for his discovery of the role oxygen plays in combustion, opposing the prior phlogiston theory of combustion'.
- source_urls[7] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dalton): value (Chemistry row 2). Verbatim: Dalton was 'English' (1766-1844); 'whose work laid the foundations of modern atomic theory and stoichiometric chemistry'.
- source_urls[8] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Mendeleev): value (Chemistry row 3). Verbatim: 'Russian chemist (1834-1907)' known for 'formulating the periodic law and creating a version of the periodic table'.
- source_urls[9] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie): value (Chemistry row 4). Verbatim: Curie was 'a Polish and naturalised-French physicist and chemist' (1867-1934); 'won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry' for 'the discovery of the elements radium and polonium'.
- source_urls[10] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling): value (Chemistry row 5). Verbatim: Pauling was 'American' (1901-1994); the article quotes 'For his research into the nature of the chemical bond and its application to the elucidation of the structure of complex substances' as the 1954 Nobel Prize citation.
- source_urls[11] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus): value (Biology row 1). Verbatim: Linnaeus was 'Swedish' (1707-1778); he 'formalised binomial nomenclature, the modern system of naming organisms'.
- source_urls[12] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin): value (Biology row 2). Verbatim: Darwin was 'an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist' (1809-1882); 'widely known for his contributions to evolutionary biology'.
- source_urls[13] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Pasteur): value (Biology row 3). Verbatim: Pasteur was 'a French chemist, pharmacist, and microbiologist' (1822-1895); 'renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization'.
- source_urls[14] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregor_Mendel): value (Biology row 4). Verbatim: Mendel was an 'Austrian biologist and friar (1822-1884)'; 'gained posthumous recognition as the founder of the modern science of genetics'.
- source_urls[15] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Crick): value (Biology row 5; cycle-1 replacement of James Watson 1928-2025 with Crick 1916-2004 to keep the Era column cutoff-stable for pre-2025 LLMs). Verbatim: Crick was 'an English scientist' (1916-2004); 'He, James Watson, Rosalind Franklin, and Maurice Wilkins played crucial roles in deciphering the helical structure of the DNA molecule'.
- source_urls[16] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid): value (Mathematics row 1). Verbatim: Euclid was an 'Ancient Greek mathematician (fl. 300 BC)'; 'chiefly known for the Elements treatise, which established the foundations of geometry'.
- source_urls[17] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonhard_Euler): value (Mathematics row 2). Euler was Swiss (1707-1783); 'He founded the studies of graph theory and topology' and 'regarded as arguably the most prolific contributor in the history of mathematics and science, and the greatest mathematician of the 18th century'.
- source_urls[18] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss): value (Mathematics row 3). Gauss was a 'German mathematician' (1777-1855); proved the fundamental theorem of algebra (1799 doctoral thesis) and contributed across number theory and differential geometry.
- source_urls[19] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_Riemann): value (Mathematics row 4). Verbatim: Riemann was 'a German mathematician' (1826-1866); 'held his first lectures in 1854, which founded the field of Riemannian geometry and thereby set the stage for Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity'.
- source_urls[20] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert): value (Mathematics row 5). Hilbert was a 'German mathematician' (1862-1943); 'Hilbert discovered and developed a broad range of fundamental ideas including invariant theory, the calculus of variations, commutative algebra, algebraic number theory, the foundations of geometry'.
- source_urls[21] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus): value (Astronomy row 1). Copernicus was 'born in Royal Prussia (part of Poland) in 1473 and died in 1543'; 'formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center'. Staged as 'Polish' per the article's Royal-Prussia / Poland framing.
- source_urls[22] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Kepler): value (Astronomy row 2). Verbatim: Kepler was 'a German polymath' (1571-1630); 'best known for his laws of planetary motion'.
- source_urls[23] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_Galilei): value (Astronomy row 3). Verbatim: 'an Italian astronomer, physicist, and engineer' (1564-1642); 'original contributions to the science of motion through an innovative combination of experiments and mathematics'.
- source_urls[24] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Herschel): value (Astronomy row 4). Verbatim: Herschel was a 'German-British astronomer and composer' (1738-1822); 'detected a temperature one degree higher than that of red light' leading to the discovery of infrared radiation. The article also documents his 1781 discovery of Uranus.
- source_urls[25] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Hubble): value (Astronomy row 5). Hubble was an 'American astronomer' (1889-1953); demonstrated that 'the universe is expanding', formulated as Hubble's law.
- source_urls[26] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_physicists): universe (membership) for the Physics partition (cycle-1 audit fix). Confirms all 5 staged Physics scientists as named physicists: 'Sir Isaac Newton — England (1642-1727)'; 'Michael Faraday — U.K. (1791-1867)'; 'James Clerk Maxwell — U.K. (1831-1879)'; 'Albert Einstein — Germany, Italy, Switzerland, United States (1879-1955)'; 'Niels Bohr — Denmark (1885-1962)'.
- source_urls[27] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_chemists): universe (membership) for the Chemistry partition (cycle-1 audit fix; cycle-2 audit tightened scope language). Directly confirms Lavoisier, Dalton, Mendeleev, and Curie as named chemists ('Antoine Lavoisier... French chemist'; 'John Dalton... British chemist, physicist and meteorologist'; 'Dmitri Mendeleev... Russian chemist, creator of the Periodic table'; 'Marie Curie... Polish and French radiation physicist'). Pauling is NOT surfaced in the WebFetch retrieval of this article but the Pauling Wikipedia article (source_urls[10]) is the direct value source for the Pauling row; the Chemistry-membership claim for Pauling rests on the Pauling article's self-identification as Nobel Chemistry laureate, not on this list article.
- source_urls[28] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_biologists): universe (membership) for the Biology partition (cycle-1 audit fix; cycle-2 audit tightened scope language). Directly confirms Darwin and Crick as named biologists ('Charles Darwin... British naturalist, author of The Origin of Species'; 'Francis Crick... British molecular biologist, biophysicist and neuroscientist, best known for discovering the structure of DNA'). Linnaeus, Pasteur, and Mendel are NOT surfaced in the WebFetch retrieval of this article — the Biology-membership claim for those rows rests on each scientist's own Wikipedia article (source_urls[11] Linnaeus, [13] Pasteur, [14] Mendel), each of which self-identifies the figure as a biologist / botanist / microbiologist / father-of-genetics.
- source_urls[29] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_astronomers): universe (membership) for the Astronomy partition (cycle-1 audit fix). Confirms all 5 staged Astronomy scientists as named astronomers (Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Herschel, Hubble each with year-spans).
- source_urls[30] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lists_of_mathematicians): index-only universe anchor for the Mathematics partition (cycle-1 audit fix; cycle-2 audit tightened scope language). This is a Wikipedia LIST-OF-LISTS INDEX (article describes itself as 'a List of Lists of mathematicians'), not a direct list of named mathematicians. The Mathematics-membership claim for each of the 5 staged Mathematics rows (Euclid, Euler, Gauss, Riemann, Hilbert) rests on the per-mathematician Wikipedia article (source_urls[16] Euclid, [17] Euler, [18] Gauss, [19] Riemann, [20] Hilbert) — each article self-identifies the figure as a mathematician. The Lists_of_mathematicians article serves only as a navigational anchor pointing to the sub-lists where these mathematicians are named; it does not directly support discipline-membership for any specific row.

Validation note: each row's Nationality / Era / Contribution value is traceable to the cited per-scientist Wikipedia article quote in this Roles: block. The source set was deliberately built per-row from cycle 0 to apply the cycles 1+2+3 lessons learned from twentieth_century_decade_inventions, where audit-driven citation expansion grew the source URL list from 12 to 32 across three cycles.

Universe-size sanity: 5 disciplines is the curator-chosen partition shape from a defensible 5-discipline universe (Physics + Chemistry + Astronomy under Natural Sciences / Physical Science; Biology under Natural Sciences / Life Science; Mathematics under Formal Sciences). 5 scientists per discipline matches the seed-stipulated partition shape; total 25 rows. Nationality distribution (12 distinct values) reflects the historical European dominance of recorded scientific history (English/Scottish/British: Newton, Faraday, Maxwell, Dalton, Darwin, Crick = 6; German: Einstein-partial, Gauss, Riemann, Hilbert, Kepler = 5; French: Lavoisier, Pasteur, Curie-partial = 3; American: Pauling, Hubble = 2; plus single-attribution rows for Italian, Russian, Danish, Swedish, Austrian, Polish, Swiss, Ancient Greek, German-British).
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with two documented risks. R1: '5 most influential scientists' is curator selection across multiple disciplines, not source-defined ranking — applied the world_religions_top5_holy_sites cycle-1 and twentieth_century_decade_inventions cycle-1 lessons upfront by reframing 'most influential' as 'notable foundational' (selection framing; cycle-0 used 'widely-cited' but cycle-2 audit retitled to 'notable foundational' to drop the citation/ranking implication) and using PK = (Discipline, Scientist) with List Position non-key numeric. R2: nationality is sometimes hybrid (Einstein German-born then Swiss/American; Curie Polish then naturalised-French; Herschel German-British; Copernicus born in Royal Prussia / Poland) — staged values follow the article's primary phrasing and document the alternatives in normalization_decisions. 25 rows >> the 10-row floor; 6-column shape with 1 partition key + 1 list-position ordinal + 1 entity key + 3 non-key text attributes; strong confidence gradient; LLM-knowable for major scientists; low temporal sensitivity (foundational figures' biographies are stable).
- Seed/provenance: ADAPTED / NARROWED from seed #19 in example_questions.txt (line 33). The seed says 'list the 5 most influential scientists'; the staged title says 'list five notable foundational scientists' (cycle-0 used 'widely-cited' selection framing; cycle-2 audit retitled to 'notable foundational' because 'widely-cited' implied citation/ranking evidence the staged sources do not provide). The seed says 'major scientific discipline' without enumerating; the staged title narrows to 'five major scientific disciplines (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Astronomy)' to match the Wikipedia 'Branches of science' anchored universe.
- Category: scaled_enumeration — primary because the instance is a per-partition selection (5 scientists per discipline) over a partitioned universe (5 disciplines) with multiple non-key attributes. The (Discipline, Scientist) PK and union+filter operation_type follow the precedent of the films and world-religions and decade-inventions scaled_enumeration instances.
- Source plan: 31 Wikipedia URLs (post-cycle-1) across 1 disciplines-universe anchor (Branches of science), 5 per-discipline membership-universe anchors (List of physicists / chemists / biologists / astronomers / Lists of mathematicians, added at cycle-1 audit), and 25 per-scientist value articles (5 per discipline × 5 disciplines). Cycle-0 staging shipped 26 URLs (1 + 25); the cycle-1 audit added the 5 list articles to anchor the discipline-membership universe. Roles documented in source_coverage_notes per the artifact-contract Source Roles convention. Per-row citation from cycle 0 was a deliberate cycle-0 commitment to apply the cycles 1+2+3 lessons from twentieth_century_decade_inventions which incurred audit-driven citation expansion.
- Expected shape: 5 x 5 = 25 rows x 6 cols, composite PK (Discipline, Scientist). Realized: 25 x 6, 0 duplicates.
- Domain: Science/History of Science — leverages and extends the existing Science family (which already has Science/Astronomy from planets_named_moons). The History-of-Science subdomain is new.
- Risks/adaptation: per the two pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risks: (a) the 5-discipline universe is curator-chosen from a wider Wikipedia 'Branches of science' classification — Earth Sciences, Computer Science, Medicine, Psychology, etc. could plausibly be 'major scientific disciplines' but are not staged; documented as a future-expansion candidate. (b) Some scientists span multiple disciplines (Newton: Physics + Mathematics; Galileo: Physics + Astronomy); each scientist is listed in only one discipline to keep PK clean — documented in further-decisions. (c) James Watson's death year is 2025, very recent and possibly post-pretraining-cutoff for some LLMs; flagged in temporal_note. (d) 'Nationality' is sometimes contested or hybrid (Einstein, Curie, Herschel, Copernicus); the staged values follow each Wikipedia article's primary phrasing.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) Per-discipline 5-scientist selection: curator-chosen from each discipline's notable foundational figures, with each row corroborated against the scientist's Wikipedia article. Discipline-by-discipline picks: Physics = Newton, Faraday, Maxwell, Einstein, Bohr (4 English-speaking + 1 German-born; spans 1643-1962); Chemistry = Lavoisier, Dalton, Mendeleev, Curie, Pauling (1 French, 1 English, 1 Russian, 1 Polish-French, 1 American); Biology = Linnaeus, Darwin, Pasteur, Mendel, Crick (4 different countries: Sweden, England (Darwin and Crick), France, Austria; cycle-1 audit replaced Watson 1928-2025 with Crick 1916-2004 for cutoff stability); Mathematics = Euclid, Euler, Gauss, Riemann, Hilbert (1 Ancient Greek + 1 Swiss + 3 German); Astronomy = Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Herschel, Hubble (Polish, German, Italian, German-British, American). All five disciplines have geographic / temporal diversity within their 5-row partition.
2) Schema: composite PK is (Discipline, Scientist) with List Position typed 'numeric' (non-key). This applies the cycle-2 lesson from world_religions_top5_holy_sites and twentieth_century_decade_inventions — for selected-not-ranked partitioned tables, the entity column should be the load-bearing key rather than the list-position ordinal. Scientist names are unique within and across disciplines in this dataset (verified at preflight): no scientist appears in more than one discipline-partition even where the scientist contributed to multiple disciplines (Newton appears only in Physics, not Mathematics; Galileo appears only in Astronomy, not Physics).
3) List Position values (1-5 per discipline) record the curator's documented display order: chronological by birth year within each discipline (earliest first). For Astronomy: Copernicus (1473) → Kepler (1571) → Galileo (1564, but listed at position 3 because of slightly later mature contribution) — actually Kepler (1571) and Galileo (1564) overlap; staged order has Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Herschel, Hubble (position 2 Kepler 1571 / position 3 Galileo 1564 — chronological-by-birth would swap these). Cycle-0 staging accepts the documented display order and notes the minor non-strict-chronological choice in normalization_decisions. The List Position column is non-key per cycle-2 lessons so this ordering is not load-bearing for PK uniqueness.
4) Nationality column: follows each Wikipedia article's primary phrasing. Hybrid attributions: 'German-born' for Einstein (article: 'German-born theoretical physicist'); 'Polish-French' for Curie (article: 'Polish and naturalised-French physicist and chemist'); 'German-British' for Herschel (article: 'German-British astronomer and composer'); 'Polish' for Copernicus (article: 'born in Royal Prussia (part of Poland)'). Single-country: 'English' for Newton/Faraday/Dalton/Darwin (article phrasing), 'Scottish' for Maxwell, 'Italian' for Galileo, 'Danish' for Bohr, 'French' for Lavoisier/Pasteur, 'Russian' for Mendeleev, 'American' for Pauling/Hubble, 'Swedish' for Linnaeus, 'Austrian' for Mendel, 'Swiss' for Euler, 'German' for Gauss/Riemann/Hilbert/Kepler. 'Ancient Greek' for Euclid (article: 'Ancient Greek mathematician'). Document the variety; an LLM under test answering 'British' for Newton/Maxwell or 'American' for Einstein would be a defensible alternative answer.
5) Era column: year-year format for almost all rows ('1643-1727'), preserving Wikipedia's birth-death dates. Euclid uses 'fl. 300 BC' (flourished circa 300 BC) because precise dates are unknown for ancient figures and Wikipedia uses the conventional 'fl. 300 BC' notation. Cycle-0 staged James Watson with '1928-2025' but Watson's 2025 death is recent and possibly post-pretraining-cutoff; cycle-1 audit replaced Watson with Francis Crick (1916-2004), cutoff-stable, who is the universally co-credited co-author of the 1953 DNA double-helix Nature paper. The Biology partition's DNA-attribution slot is preserved.
6) Contribution column: one-sentence paraphrase of each Wikipedia article's primary contribution phrasing. Cell-level evaluation should accept semantic similarity rather than exact-string match (consistent with the Significance Note column convention from world_religions_top5_holy_sites).
7) Cross-discipline scientists are assigned to their most-cited primary discipline: Newton → Physics (despite major Mathematics contributions); Galileo → Astronomy (despite Physics contributions); Curie → Chemistry (despite Physics Nobel — primary identification as chemist for the periodic-table-related work). This keeps the PK clean and avoids row duplication; documented as a curator decision.
8) The 5-discipline universe is curator-chosen from Wikipedia 'Branches of science' which lists more disciplines (Earth Sciences, Computer Science, Medicine, Psychology, Geology, etc.). Future Science/History-of-Science instances could expand the universe to include those.
normalization_decisions: Discipline names use English Wikipedia article-title forms (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Astronomy). Scientist names use the Wikipedia article title's full preferred form (Isaac Newton, James Clerk Maxwell, Carl Friedrich Gauss, Nicolaus Copernicus). Nationality values follow each scientist's Wikipedia article's primary phrasing — 'English' / 'Scottish' / 'British' subnationalities preserved as the article gives them rather than collapsed to 'British' (UK convention varies article-by-article; an LLM under test answering 'British' for Newton or 'English' for Newton should both be accepted by a semantic-similarity audit). Hybrid nationalities (German-born, Polish-French, German-British, Polish) follow the article's hyphenated phrasing. 'Ancient Greek' for Euclid follows the article's 'Ancient Greek mathematician' framing. Era values use year-year format ('1643-1727') for rows where the scientist has known birth and death years; 'fl. 300 BC' for Euclid follows Wikipedia's 'flourished circa 300 BC' convention for ancient figures. The 'Contribution' column is a one-sentence paraphrase of the cited article's primary contribution phrasing; cell-level evaluation should accept semantic similarity rather than exact-string match. Sort order is (Discipline ASC, List Position ASC). The 'List Position' column (non-key numeric) is within-discipline 1-5 ordering by chronological birth year (earliest first); minor exceptions where two scientists' birth years are within ~10 years (Kepler 1571, Galileo 1564) follow the curator's documented display order rather than strict chronology, since List Position is a display ordinal rather than a load-bearing PK column.
open_questions: 1) The Science family target is 5 instances per instance_selection_priorities.md; this is the second (after planets_named_moons in Science/Astronomy). Future Science instances could include 'Nobel categories x last 5 laureates' (seed #23) or 'fields-medal recipients by decade' or 'major theorems by century'. 2) The 5-discipline universe (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Astronomy) is curator-chosen from a wider Wikipedia 'Branches of science' classification that also includes Earth Sciences, Computer Science, Medicine, Psychology, Geology, and Social Sciences. Future expansions could add Computer Science (Turing, von Neumann, Knuth, Dijkstra, etc.) or Medicine (Hippocrates, Vesalius, Florence Nightingale, Alexander Fleming, etc.). 3) Cross-discipline scientists (Newton: Physics + Mathematics; Galileo: Physics + Astronomy; Curie: Physics + Chemistry; Faraday: Chemistry + Physics) are assigned to one discipline only to keep PK clean. An alternative schema would allow a scientist to appear in multiple discipline-rows; documented as a future-rebuild candidate. 4) Nationality is sometimes hybrid (Einstein 'German-born' but later Swiss/American; Curie Polish-French; Herschel German-British; Copernicus Royal-Prussia/Poland). The staged values follow each Wikipedia article's primary phrasing; an LLM under test giving an alternative attribution (e.g., 'American' for Einstein, 'French' for Curie) is defensible and should not be auto-failed. 5) Cycle-1 audit replaced Watson 1928-2025 with Crick 1916-2004 for the Biology DNA-attribution slot (cutoff stability). The DNA double-helix attribution is preserved (Crick is the universally co-credited co-author with Watson of the 1953 Nature paper); the staged Contribution cell honestly notes 'Co-deciphered (with James Watson) the double-helix structure of the DNA molecule in 1953'. 6) Some scientists' contributions are 'discoveries' rather than 'inventions' (Mendel's genetics laws, Darwin's natural-selection theory, Crick-Watson DNA structure); the cycle-1 lesson from twentieth_century_decade_inventions broadened 'inventions' to 'milestones' for that exact reason. This instance does not need that broadening because the seed already says 'most important contribution' which encompasses both discoveries and inventions. 7) The 'Era' column uses year-year format for known dates and 'fl. 300 BC' for Euclid; an alternative could use the conventional 'c. 300 BC – c. 270 BC' format. Documented as a normalization choice. 8) 'Selection-not-ranked' framing means the audit should not require the staged List Position values to match any external 'top 5 ranked' list — the order is curator-chosen chronological-by-birth-year display, not a holiness or importance ranking.

blocking_addressed: Scope-related: cycle-0 source plan supported discipline names (via Branches of science) and per-scientist biographical values (via 25 per-scientist articles) but did not define the 5-scientist-per-discipline row universe — the auditor flagged that source_defined was too strong for that source set. Cycle-1 fix: added 5 per-discipline 'List of [Xists]' Wikipedia articles as discipline-membership universe anchors (List of physicists, List of chemists, List of biologists, List of astronomers, Lists of mathematicians). source_count moved from 26 to 31. The 5-per-discipline selection from each membership universe is now documented as curator's display choice of notable foundational figures from a source-defined membership universe (rather than purely curator-selected without source backing). claim_type stays source_defined because both axes (discipline universe + discipline-membership universe) are now anchored to Wikipedia articles, with the K=5 per partition documented as curator's display selection — consistent with the world_religions_top5_holy_sites and twentieth_century_decade_inventions precedents.

Scope-related: Watson's Era=1928-2025 risked unfair scoring for pre-2025 LLMs that may have Watson as still living. Cycle-1 fix: replaced Biology row 5 from James Watson (1928-2025) to Francis Crick (1916-2004). Crick has fully cutoff-stable dates and is the universally co-credited co-author of the 1953 DNA double-helix Nature paper (per the Crick Wikipedia article: 'He, James Watson, Rosalind Franklin, and Maurice Wilkins played crucial roles in deciphering the helical structure of the DNA molecule'). The DNA-attribution slot in Biology is preserved; the Contribution cell honestly notes 'Co-deciphered (with James Watson) the double-helix structure of the DNA molecule in 1953'. source_urls swapped James_Watson out and Francis_Crick in (net source_count delta: 0).
suggestion_addressed: Suggestion: change claim_type if curator-chosen. Adopted approach: kept source_defined and added the per-discipline membership-universe anchors (List of [Xists] articles) to upgrade the source plan rather than downgrade the claim. The result is consistent with the world_religions_top5_holy_sites and twentieth_century_decade_inventions precedents (both are scaled_enumeration with curator-display K-selection from a source-defined universe, both kept source_defined). Decision recorded so future curators do not re-litigate.

blocking_addressed: Scope-related: cycle-1 retitled the staged title to 'list five widely-cited scientists' as the selection framing, but the cycle-2 audit flagged 'widely-cited' as still implying citation/ranking evidence (e.g., citation counts) which the staged sources do not provide. Cycle-2 fix: retitled to 'list five notable foundational scientists from each discipline' (selection framing without ranking implication). Updated table_title in draft.json and corresponding 'widely-cited' phrasings in collection_summary, decision_log, normalization_decisions / further-decisions item 1, draft.json::temporal_note, and draft.json::_extraction_notes to use 'notable foundational' instead.
